agent_notes: צֶדֶק is the crux. KJV/ASV 'Hear the right' takes it as the object of 'hear' (a just cause); YLT 'Hear, O Jehovah, righteousness' leaves it bare; the Targum and Ibn Ezra, Radak, Metzudat David read it adverbially or as describing the prayer ('in righteousness', 'a prayer that is righteous'). I keep it as the object of 'hear' in the literal layer and let the dramatic layer carry both senses.
The title 'A prayer of David' is verse 1 in the Hebrew numbering (KJV 17:0 and 17:1 together). The Hebrew has no separate title verse: תְּפִלָּה לְדָוִד is the first clause of the verse.
Gloss of רִנָּתִי: STEPBible 'cry of entreaty'. Radak and Ibn Ezra stress that rinnah is a loud cry (sometimes of joy, here of entreaty). I gloss 'my cry'; the parallel with tefillah is kept visible.

Superscription and the traditional reading: Rashi, Radak and Meiri read this psalm against David and Bathsheba (2 Sam 11), others against Saul. I do not decide; I name both readings in the commentary of verses where the commentators divide (vv. 2, 3, 12). The dramatic layer does not choose either.

חֶלְבָּמוֹ סָגְרוּ: the object is fronted. Either 'their fat they have closed' (they have shut up their own hearts or mouths with fat) or, as KJV/ASV/BBE, 'they are enclosed in their fat', a reflexive that the Hebrew does not have. Ibn Ezra offers both (fat closed up inside them, or they closed [their mouths] with fat). Rashi: they closed their hearts and eyes with their fat. I keep the Hebrew order and leave the object ambiguous.

Revised per request: 'this translation follows the Qere'. Radak says the Ketiv is singular ('me') and the Qere plural ('us'); Meiri reports it the other way round (written plural, read singular). Only Radak is cited for the assignment. Note that the verb in the packet's printed Hebrew is the plural form.

(PS.17.11 commentary: "but the tradition reads 'us' (Qere), and the packet's gloss follows the reading")

agent_notes: דִּמְיֹנוֹ is singular ('his likeness'): the enemies of v. 9–11 were plural, and now one stands for them. Radak and Meiri identify him as Saul (citing Ps 7:3); Ibn Ezra says each of the encircling men. I preserve the singular in both layers.

יִכְסוֹף: KJV 'greedy of his prey' reads the Hebrew as 'it longs'; kasaf is 'to long, yearn' (Rashi cites Gen 31:30 'you longed, longed'). So the lion is not greedy but yearning: I keep the verb of longing.

The final phrase 'from the wicked, your sword' is ambiguous: 'your sword' may be in apposition (the wicked man IS your sword; Rashi, Radak, Malbim, Targum 'condemned to be killed by your sword' differs) or instrumental ('by your sword'; Meiri's second option, ASV, BBE). I kept the apposition in the literal layer, which follows the Hebrew order, and the dramatic layer keeps it too. The five English versions split exactly here.

STEPBible glosses פַּלְּטָה as 'deliver !' and הַכְרִיעֵהוּ as 'make bow down him'; I kept both. קַדְּמָה פָנָיו is literally 'go before his face'; whether this is 'confront' (ASV) or 'forestall' (Meiri, Metzudat David) is a judgment call, and I give the literal layer 'meet his face'.

Revised per request: the sentence calling 'the dead' a misreading is gone. Two readings of mittim are now given: 'men of this world' (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Malbim) and 'those who die by God's hand', whose portion is the world to come (Rashi, Metzudat David, Targum), with Meiri's tribal reading. The translation layers keep 'men', which is the grammatically plain reading, and the reader is told the other exists. Radak's report of the Berakhot 61b midrash is also noted. The dramatic layer's 'nothing past it' follows Radak's reading.

agent_notes: Verse 3 is very hard. The consonantal zammoti can be 'I have resolved / purposed' (verb zamam) or 'my plan/scheme' (noun zimmah, as YLT 'My thoughts'). KJV 'I am purposed' follows the verb; I follow it too. The last clause is also divided: 'my mouth shall not transgress' (KJV) vs 'my plan does not pass beyond my mouth' (YLT, Ibn Ezra, Metzudat David: thought and speech agree). I keep 'my mouth' as subject of ya'avor, as the Hebrew has it.

בַּל תִּמְצָא: KJV 'and shalt find nothing' supplies 'nothing' as object; the Hebrew has no object. I mark it in brackets. Rashi reads 'you did not find your desire in me'; Ibn Ezra 'a fault or blemish'; Radak 'you did not find me unclean'.

STEPBible glosses צְרַפְתַּנִי as 'you have tested me'; the lexical sense is 'refine, smelt' (metal). The literal layer keeps 'you have smelted me' for the metallurgical image; Metzudat David also reads it as a smelter testing silver.

history.note: [consider] Render 'you will not find [anything]'. Also, Meiri gives the Bathsheba reading first and the general reading second, so 'Meiri reads it as a general statement' is half the picture. (PS.17.3: "צְרַפְתַּנִי בַל־תִּמְצָא")

agent_notes: Verse 4 is syntactically unresolved. 'As for the deeds of humankind, by the word of your lips I have kept myself from the paths of the violent' (KJV, ASV) is the common reading; Radak and Meiri give a second reading in which David also restrains others. Malbim reads it as a continuation of the preceding verbs. The Hebrew says only 'I have watched/kept the paths of the violent person', with no 'from'; the 'from' is KJV's smoothing. I bracket it.
